intended: "Pass rates cover the students entered for the exam", while the same line records that "about a quarter of each cohort's roll was not entered". The claim is about the cohorts given the tutoring blocks, so the population is every student on the roll, not the entered fraction alone. Students held back from entry are the weakest candidates, and removing them raises the pass rate among those who remain, which is enough to produce a 4 to 8 point rise with no change in what any student learned. All four cohorts are algebra at Brantwood College in one spring term, so the entry rule applies identically across the four cases and none of them corrects the others.
reported: The numbers cover a narrower population than the claim: 'Pass rates cover the students entered for the exam, and about a quarter of each cohort's roll was not entered', with no rule filling in the non-entered students. Withholding the weakest quarter of each roll from entry raises the pass rate mechanically, so the 4-8 point gains need not reflect any improvement in the cohorts the tutoring blocks were given to.

reported: "Pass rates cover the students entered for the exam, and about a quarter of each cohort's roll was not entered" - the 4-8 point rises are measured on only the entered three-quarters of each cohort, so entry decisions (e.g. holding weaker students back) could produce the whole gain, and the figure does not describe the cohorts the claim is about.

intended: All four groups are the 12-17 band at Harrowfield inside one winter quarter, so a single district air history covers every case at once. The mid-passage facts state that pollen and airborne irritants in each group's district fell by half from the previous quarter and that every group lived and slept in unfiltered district air, so the cleaner air reached every patient whose attacks were counted. Each band is compared against itself a quarter earlier rather than against an untreated band in the same quarter, so the drop in irritants and the inhaler moved together and the 4 to 7 attack reductions cannot be attributed to the inhaler. The population and completeness clauses in the same line describe a count with no gap between the patients tallied and the patients the claim covers, so the drop in irritants is the whole of the defect.
reported: 'Pollen and airborne irritants in each group's district fell by half from the previous quarter, and every group lived and slept in unfiltered district air' - a named alternative cause that changed between the compared quarters and demonstrably reached every one of the four groups, so the 4-7 fewer attacks cannot be attributed to the inhaler.

intended: The mid-passage line tallies the infection rates over the patients discharged from each ward, and the clause beside it records that each ward transferred out a quarter of those admitted. The claim is about ward infection rates, which is a claim about everyone the ward admitted, so a quarter of that population sits outside the numbers entirely. Patients who deteriorate are the ones moved to intensive care or to another hospital, and infection is a common reason for that move, so the excluded quarter is precisely where infections would concentrate and the reported drop is measured over the patients who did well enough to leave by the front door. All four entries are Ashgrove General's surgical ward in the first quarter and each drops the same quarter, so nothing in the file recovers the transferred patients.
reported: The infection numbers 'cover the patients discharged from each ward' while 'each ward transferred out a quarter of those admitted', so a quarter of admissions - plausibly the sicker, more infection-prone ones - never enter the rate at all. The measured population is narrower than the ward infection rate the claim is about, and a shift in who gets transferred would move the figure by itself.

The 6-11 percent drop is about a narrower population than the claimed 'ward infection rates'.

intended: The mid-passage line states that figures cover the orders that cleared the staffed tills, and that about a fifth of each store's orders went through self-checkout. The revenue-per-order numbers are therefore tallied over roughly four fifths of the orders on each line, while the claim is about revenue per order on the repriced lines as a whole, self-checkout baskets included. Self-checkout baskets are a systematically different set of purchases from staffed-till baskets, typically smaller and quicker, so the 6, 4, 7 and 5 percent gains recorded on the staffed-till subset are consistent with revenue per order across all orders holding flat or falling. Every case is coffee at Harlow Street inside March under lead Vasquez, so the same excluded fifth sits under all four cases and no case in the log covers it.
reported: Revenue per order is measured on a narrower population than the claim: "Figures cover the orders that cleared the staffed tills, and about a fifth of each store's orders went through self-checkout." Roughly 20 percent of orders are excluded, and self-checkout baskets differ systematically in size, so the 4-7 percent rise need not hold for revenue per order overall.

intended: In cases one and three the heart rate was read before the app was started: 29 March precedes 4 April, and 30 September precedes 5 October. Half the evidence therefore describes a drop that had already happened when the app was taken up, so it cannot be evidence for the app. The two remaining cases, two and four, are not enough on their own.
reported: Two of the four cases measure the outcome before the intervention began: cohort One "started 4 April; by 29 March resting heart rate ran 5 bpm below", and cohort Three "started 5 October; by 30 September ... 6 bpm below". The drop is dated prior to enrollment, so the app cannot have caused it.
